author: Shereen Siewert
title: Wausau council will take up a citywide audit, with public comment first on the agenda - NewsBreak
text:
By Shereen Siewert ,
8 hours ago Wausau City Council meeting from June 9, 2026. Source: Wausau Area Access Media sceengrab WAUSAU, Wis. — The Wausau Common Council will convene a special session to consider commissioning an independent audit of city operations, and residents will get the first word at it.
Council President Terry Kilian said she received a written request Sunday afternoon from District 7 Alder Matt Hoenecke, submitted on behalf of himself and District 11 Alder Bruce Trueblood, asking for a Committee of the Whole “to consider and vote on pursuing a comprehensive, independent audit of city operations.” Kilian said she is working with the mayor and alders to set a date.
Mayor Doug Diny confirmed he received the same request. “I will work with Council President Kilian to place the matter on a Committee of the Whole agenda,” he wrote.
She also said she will place public comment first on the agenda, so residents who cannot stay for an entire meeting can still be heard.
“It is my feeling that Wausau is at a critical point with its financial status,” Kilian wrote, “and I would support moving ahead with the audit realizing that the time demands may be increased.”
A Committee of the Whole is a meeting of all 11 alders sitting together, outside the usual committee structure, to work through a single subject at length. It can be scheduled by the mayor, by the council president, or at the request of any two alders — which is how this one arrived. Hoenecke asked that the audit be the session’s sole focus, and Kilian said she supports that.
The session is for discussion and possible action, Kilian said, and its authority has limits. A Committee of the Whole can vote to send items forward to the full council, but it cannot set policy itself. As chair, she said, she will review and sign the agenda, and has asked the requesting alders to provide their agenda proposals and packet materials.
How wide, and how soon Agreeing to hold the meeting is not the same as agreeing on what should come out of it, and the responses so far describe two different reviews.
Diny said he is open to an “independent operational or performance review of selected city functions” if the council believes it would add value beyond the annual financial audit, which he said will be presented in September. Any such review, he wrote, “should have a clearly defined scope, measurable objectives, a realistic cost estimate, and a timeline that does not compromise core operations or the preparation of the 2027 budget.”
He also favors doing it in stages. “The most productive approach is sequential,” he wrote, describing changes already underway to budget reporting and presentation, made at council members’ request and limited by what the city’s budget software can do. A broader review, he wrote, “should begin with a carefully developed scope and clear priorities so that effort and cost remain focused and efficient.”
Diny said he has tried before. In prior budget cycles, he wrote, he advanced concepts for zero-based budgeting elements and targeted operational studies with the finance director’s support, and “those proposals did not advance at the time.”
Trueblood has described something considerably larger: an outside organization with no existing relationship with the city, examining every department and every major process over one to two years. Kilian, asked about the timing concern, said she understands it but believes the city should proceed regardless. Finance Committee Chair Michael Martens said he would support a review if its scope and purpose were defined and if it does not collide with the November budget deadline.
Those differences are what the Committee of the Whole will have to resolve.
How Wausau got here The audit push follows a Wausau Pilot & Review investigation, published this month, into how the city accounts for its spending in the budget document residents see.
Wausau’s budget book prints tables labeled “Budgetary History” for every department and every fund. Those tables do not contain spending history. They repeat what the council adopted in prior years, under columns headed “Expenses” and “Revenues,” with nothing on the page explaining the difference — a construction that departs from national standards for budget documents.
In the Motor Pool Fund, which buys the city’s police cars, plows, ambulances and fire engines, the tables show $57.9 million in spending over the past decade. Actual spending, verified against the city’s own budget books and audited financial statements, was roughly $14 million lower. The fund needed borrowed money three times in five years to stay afloat, and the 2026 budget defers replacing an aerial fire truck and an ambulance.
Diny has since confirmed an error in one of the tables and directed the Finance Department to examine presenting actual prior-year figures in the 2027 executive budget. Finance Director Maryanne Groat said the 2027 book will carry a 10-year history.
Asked afterward where they stood, six of the council’s 11 members told Wausau Pilot & Review they support an independent audit. None said they oppose one.
What the alders want examined Trueblood, in a letter to the editor published Saturday, described a review he estimates could take one to two years, conducted by an outside organization with no existing relationship with the city, covering every department and every major process.
It should look beyond finances to the city’s governance and organizational structure, he wrote: “Who answers to whom? What practices have become standard? Do they comply with state statutes? Are they consistent with accepted municipal best practices, or are we simply doing things the way we have always done them?”
Trueblood said he was told at a council meeting that Wausau’s last comprehensive audit of this kind was in the late 1990s.
Diny gave a different account of the city’s history with outside reviews. The most recent operational study, he said, was the Mercury Associates examination of the Motor Pool, delivered in April 2021. Earlier reviews, under former Mayor Linda Lawrence, were conducted department by department rather than as a single citywide engagement, he wrote, the last of them a review of the Police Department.
If that is right, Wausau may never have commissioned the kind of comprehensive, citywide review Trueblood and Hoenecke are asking for. Wausau Pilot & Review has filed a public records request seeking the most recent such review and any past council actions commissioning one. Diny said that request “is the appropriate channel for locating any remaining materials.”
The city’s experience with the study it did commission is part of the backdrop. Mercury told the city in 2021 to fix the rates it charges departments, fill vacant mechanic positions, add a fleet analyst and begin reporting fleet performance publicly. Most of those recommendations were not carried out.
Hoenecke’s stated concern is narrower and procedural: “whether or not we have the necessary processes in place to ensure public officials and residents are provided with information that is transparent, discernible, and useful when making decisions.” An audit, he wrote, “should be the start of stronger oversight, not a substitute for it.”
Martens has put the timing concern in concrete terms: the council must adopt a budget by its second November meeting for property tax bills to go out on schedule, and “proper audits take time.” The finance staff who would be central to any examination of budget preparation are the same staff producing the 2027 budget this fall.
Kilian said what the session cannot settle on its own. “I cannot say at this time — until we have a thorough discussion at the Committee of the Whole — what will need to be included in that audit,” she wrote. “We need to have more information and hear the voices of all the alders in order to make those decisions.”
A date has not been set.
summary: Diny said he is open to an “independent operational or performance review of selected city functions” if the council believes it would add value beyond the annual financial audit, which he said will be presented in September. Any such review, he wrote, “should have a clearly defined scope, measurable objectives, a realistic cost estimate, and a timeline that does not compromise core operations or the preparation of the 2027 budget.” He also favors doing it in stages.
